hint: This is a standard result to memorise.
explanation:
The standard result: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$.

All angles are measured in radians for this rule to hold.

hint: The derivative of $\cos x$ introduces a negative sign.
explanation:
The standard result: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x$.

The negative sign is easy to forget — note that differentiating twice cycles back: $\sin x \to \cos x \to -\sin x \to -\cos x \to \sin x$.

hint: The derivative of $\tan x$ involves $\sec^2 x$.
explanation:
The standard result: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x) = \sec^2 x$.

Recall that $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$, so $\sec^2 x = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x}$.

hint: Apply the chain rule: differentiate $\sin u$ to get $\cos u$, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function $u = 3x$.
Use the chain rule with inner function $u = x^2$.

stem: Find the gradient of $y = \sin x$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$. Give an exact answer as a decimal to 2 decimal places.
hint: Differentiate to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos x$, then evaluate at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Apply the chain rule: the inner function is $\dfrac{x}{2}$, which has derivative $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Chain rule with inner function $u = 2x + 1$: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan u) = \sec^2 u \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$.

stem: The function $f(x) = 3\sin(2x)$ has a stationary point in the interval $0 < x < \pi$. Find the $x$-value (in radians) of the first stationary point to 3 decimal places.
hint: Differentiate $f(x)$, set $f'(x) = 0$, and solve $\cos(2x) = 0$ for $x$ in $0 < x < \pi$.
explanation:
$f'(x) = 6\cos(2x)$.

Set $f'(x) = 0$: $\cos(2x) = 0$, so $2x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \ldots$

In $0 < x < \pi$, the first solution is $2x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, giving:
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785 \text{ radians}$$

stem: Find the gradient of $y = \cos(x^2)$ at $x = \sqrt{\pi}$. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
hint: Use the chain rule to differentiate, then substitute $x = \sqrt{\pi}$.
Differentiate twice. First find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, then differentiate again.
explanation:
First derivative: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3\cos(3x)$.

Second derivative: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 3 \times (-\sin(3x)) \times 3 = -9\sin(3x)$.

Note: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -9y$, which means $y = \sin(3x)$ satisfies a simple harmonic equation.

stem: A particle moves so that its displacement is $x(t) = 2\cos(3t) + 1$ metres at time $t$ seconds. Find the velocity (in m/s) of the particle at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ seconds.
hint: Velocity is $v(t) = x'(t)$. Differentiate $x(t)$ with respect to $t$, then substitute $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
explanation:
$v(t) = x'(t) = -2\sin(3t) \times 3 = -6\sin(3t)$.

At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$v\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -6\sin\!\left(3 \times \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -6\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -6 \times 1 = -6 \text{ m/s}$$

The negative sign means the particle is moving in the negative direction.
